theirs.title: Published by the town, the district and the state
theirs.blurb: Primary documents. We did not write any of these and we did not commission them. 45 came from the Town by records request and say so on their row; one more was handed over by somebody acting in a town role, and they are named on its row; the rest were already public. 44 of them link back to the exact file the publisher put up, and 28 of those addresses have been checked the only way an address can be — by downloading what is there now and matching it against our copy, byte for byte. A link that merely looks right is not a source. 57 still have no address of their own, and they are three different things: state reports built on form submission, where the page and the jurisdiction are the whole answer; a table we built here from a document that is itself listed above; and documents gathered before the mirror existed, where nobody wrote down where they came from. Only the last is a gap, it is a gap on our side and not the town’s, and it is named in notes/findings/DATA-WANTED.md. Where a document is unreadable or says something inconvenient, it is here anyway.

reference.title: Everything else the district and the town publish
reference.blurb: Mirrored here so it is available and so no figure has to be looked up over the network. 2208 of these 2224 feed no number on this site. The other 16 are byte-identical copies of primary sources listed above — kept, and marked as such on their row, because a mirror with the load-bearing documents quietly removed is no longer a copy of the publisher’s page. It is all here because a document nobody kept is a document nobody can check, and because we would rather hold what we did not use than be asked why we did not look.

ours.title: Written by this project, not by the town
ours.blurb: Everything below this line is ours. It is not town information, it carries no official standing, and nobody at the district or the Town has reviewed or approved it. It is one resident’s reading of the documents above, published so it can be argued with — which means checked against those documents, and disagreed with where the reading is wrong.

groups.title: State staffing and spending counts
groups.blurb: What the state records Lunenburg employing and spending, by year. It carries the quantity the district’s own budget documents cannot give: how many paraprofessionals there are.

items.title: 603 CMR 28.00 — the special education regulations
items.what: The rule that constrains special education staffing, and it is cited by no document this town publishes: across all 3,877 documents here the only "603 CMR" references are 35, 4 and 7 — educator evaluation and licensure. 28.06(6)(d) sets the class-size rule everybody argues around without quoting: a substantially separate group may not exceed eight students to one certified special educator, or twelve to a special educator AND AN AIDE — so a paraprofessional is partly what PERMITS a larger group rather than being a ratio in itself. Three qualifications travel with it and are easy to drop: these are MAXIMUMS and districts are expected to go smaller for complex needs (28.06(6)(c)); grouping must match each student’s own IEP (b); and a group at maximum may take two more students mid-year by decision of the Administrator of Special Education (e). Saved from the state’s own page rather than published as a file.

items.title: Staffing and spending by category, FY09–FY25
items.what: Massachusetts DESE, via the state open-data portal. Teacher FTE, paraprofessional FTE, in-district pupils, per-pupil expenditure by function and student demographics, every year since 2009. The paraprofessional count is the one figure that lets a budget line be read as staffing rather than as dollars — and it says the para budget has grown roughly six times faster than the number of paras. Rebuild with scripts/fetch_dese.py.

groups.title: Who lives here — the American Community Survey
groups.blurb: The Census Bureau’s five-year estimates for Lunenburg: age, households with children, income by age of householder, and owner against renter — plus median household income for every Massachusetts municipality. EVERY FIGURE IS A SAMPLE ESTIMATE WITH A MARGIN, which is what makes it a different kind of document from a DESE count of children.

items.title: Median household income, every Massachusetts municipality, 2019–2023
items.what: Fetched whole rather than for Lunenburg alone, because a rank is a claim about 350 other places and quoting one from a query nobody kept is a derived thing passed off as an observed one. Four municipalities are top-coded at $250,001 with no computable margin.

items.title: Age by sex, Lunenburg, 2019–2023
items.what: The raw API response, saved as returned. 49 estimates with their margins: every five-year age band for each sex, which is where the 65-and-over count comes from — it is a sum of twelve cells and its margin is the root of the sum of their squares, not one of theirs.

items.title: Households by presence of a child under 18, Lunenburg, 2019–2023
items.what: The real denominator behind “about 30% of homes have a child in the school”. It counts households with a child under 18 — which includes Monty Tech, private, charter and pre-school children — so it is a CEILING on the claim rather than the figure.

items.title: Owner and renter households by the year the householder moved in, Lunenburg, 2019–2023
items.what: How long the owners have been here, in bands. The question behind “taxed out of a house bought decades ago”, and the table /homes-and-taxes reads.

items.title: Median household income by age of householder, Lunenburg, 2019–2023
items.what: What turns “seniors on fixed incomes” from a claim into a number. Five estimates; the under-25 band is published as the sentinel -666666666, which means not available and is not a figure.

items.title: Owner against renter, Lunenburg, 2019–2023
items.what: Tenure. It is how a levy increase reaching four households in five directly stops being an impression.

items.title: Median year the householder moved in, Lunenburg, 2019–2023

groups.title: What neighboring districts did
groups.blurb: Primary FY27 budget documents from comparable districts. The comparison is only fair if it comes from their own books rather than from reporting.

items.title: Groton-Dunstable FY27 budget book
items.what: 132 pages. Three consecutive years of cuts, a budget below level service, and an override the district says is needed "now and in the foreseeable future". Also states plainly that it plans to offset $2M of costs with circuit breaker funding.

items.title: Ashburnham-Westminster FY27 budget
items.what: The district that made the opposite choice — explicitly preserved athletics, arts and music, and cut two elementary teaching positions instead.

items.title: Munis General Ledger procedures, version 2020.2 (hosted by Framingham, MA)
items.what: Not a Lunenburg document. Tyler’s own General Ledger procedural documentation for Munis 2020.2, served by the City of Framingham under the filename “Procedures GL 2020.2.pdf”; the document itself does not name Framingham. The fullest description held of the YTD Budget Report: every option on its screens, which years it can reach, and the option that prints the full account number. A Massachusetts town’s copy, so probably the closest of the four guides to the version Lunenburg runs -- which is a guess, not a fact.

items.title: North Middlesex budget summit notes
items.what: A $64,000 deficit at 3% growth against $1.5M at 5%. Roughly 30% of students receive special education, far above the state average.

items.title: Tyler MUNIS guide: Inquiries & Reports (CNMI Department of Finance)
items.what: Not a Lunenburg document and not a peer. A Tyler MUNIS user guide for general ledger inquiries and reports, published by the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands Department of Finance (publisher’s filename “munis-rg-inquiries-reports.pdf”). It walks through the YTD Budget Report screen by screen, with journal detail, and the standard purchase order reports. Held because Lunenburg runs the same system and publishes no guide to it: it is how a resident learns what to ask the Town for. Option names are as the CNMI’s version prints them and Lunenburg’s may differ. Filed here because of how it reached us -- another government’s own website.

items.title: Montachusett Regional admissions lottery, class of 2030
items.what: Not a peer — the district Lunenburg PAYS, and the larger of the two outflows of resident students. Filed here because of how it reached us: mirrored from another district’s own website. The summary page is trustworthy and the per-applicant pages are not: the 18 town figures sum to the printed total of 365, but the applicant pages are OCR of an image PDF and produced “L.unenburg”, “Lunchburg” and truncated statuses, so accepted-versus-waitlisted must not be counted from them. The document holds no personal data: a town, an anonymous applicant number and a status.

items.title: Ashburnham-Westminster line detail
items.what: The line-item version of the same budget.

items.title: Ayer-Shirley FY27 expenses
items.what: Level-service budget by function. Health insurance up 14.4% — the steepest in the group.

items.title: Wachusett FY27 budget presentation
items.what: Member-town assessments, enrollment by town, and a discretionary contribution up 9.21%.

items.title: Tyler MUNIS Basic User Guide 1: Overview (City of Burlingame, CA)
items.what: Not a Lunenburg document. The City of Burlingame Finance department’s introductory MUNIS guide (publisher’s filename “Tyler Munis Basic User Guide 1 - Overview.pdf”). Cited for one table: the search wildcards, where | means or and : or .. a range, which is how several funds are asked for in one run.

items.title: Instructions for MUNIS Payroll reports (Livingston County)
items.what: Not a Lunenburg document. A payroll-report guide whose own screenshots read “Munis [Livingston County]” (publisher’s filename “Instructions-MUNIS-Payroll-Reports-0823.pdf”). Held only for its generic export steps: the Excel button and the Munis Office Export Filter, which exports only the fields left selected. Nothing in it is about Lunenburg payroll.

groups.title: The assessors’ parcels — every property, as the state publishes it
groups.blurb: MassGIS’s Level 3 parcel package for Lunenburg: parcel polygons and the assessor’s FY2026 extract, joined by LOC_ID. Value, use code, year built, last recorded deed and price for all 5,303 parcels. Owner names are in the file, are public record, and are used here in aggregate only.

items.title: Level 3 parcels, Lunenburg (M162), FY2026
items.what: Downloaded 13 September 2026 from MassGIS’s direct file address. The assessing table is M162Assess_CY26_FY26.dbf; the last-sale date is a deed, not an arrival — a third are nominal transfers.

items.title: Where it came from, and what LS_DATE is not
items.what: The address, the hash, and the caveat that governs every tenure figure read from it.

groups.title: Free cash, certified — Lunenburg and eight comparable towns
groups.blurb: The Division of Local Services publishes a Free Cash Proof for every community: the year-end calculation of what a town may appropriate without raising taxes, broken into its components. Downloaded 30 August 2026. These reconcile to themselves twice over — 81 checks across nine towns and five years, all tying to the dollar. They carry no denominator of any kind, so the absolute figures do not compare between towns of different size; the composition, being a share, does.

items.title: The cherry sheet: every line of state aid and every state assessment
items.what: All 351 municipalities and all 87 regional school districts, FY2010–FY2027, receipts and assessments, 40 programmes — 235,254 figures. It answers what nothing else here could: REGIONAL TRANSPORTATION, $88.2M statewide in FY2026 and paid only to regional districts, which is the money behind the regionalisation argument. It also carries school choice tuition received and paid, and charter sending tuition and reimbursement, which is where a large part of the difference between districts’ grant and revolving income turns out to live. Long, a row per place per programme, because which programmes exist changes by year.

items.title: Health insurance expenditures, every municipality, FY2002–FY2026
items.what: DLS Gateway export, fetched by script (fetch_dls_property.py): the whole Commonwealth, one figure per town per year, from Schedule A Parts 2 and 6. Extracted to data/dls-health-insurance.csv, where the two warnings DLS prints about what the figure contains are recorded.

items.title: Assessed Values by Class, eleven towns, FY2002–FY2026
items.what: DLS Gateway export, fetched by script on 16 September 2026 (fetch_dls_property.py records the exact POST). Per town per year: residential, open space, commercial, industrial and personal property value, the total, and the residential and CIP shares. How big the commercial base IS — a revaluation moves it as much as a building does, so read it with new_growth.xlsx, which is what was added.

items.title: Average Single-Family Tax Bill, eleven towns, FY1988–FY2026
items.what: DLS Gateway export, fetched by script on 13 September 2026 (fetch_dls_tax_bills.py records the exact POST). Per town per year: single-family parcels, average value, average bill, the bill as a share of value and of income per capita, and the town’s rank among the 351. The only series in the archive that puts Lunenburg’s bill beside its neighbours’.

items.title: New Growth, residential and total, eleven towns, FY2003–FY2026
items.what: DLS Gateway export, fetched by script on 16 September 2026 (fetch_dls_property.py). Per town per year: residential new-growth value and the levy dollars it added, the same for all classes together, the prior year’s levy limit and the addition as a share of it. Total minus residential is what was BUILT that was not housing. The town’s own six-year series in model/taxbase.py is these figures, to the dollar.

items.title: Lunenburg free cash proof, 2021–2025
items.what: Certified free cash rose from $2,666,962 to $3,354,370 over the five years. Two thirds of the 2025 figure is money appropriated and not spent.

items.title: Override and underride votes, extracted
items.what: The workbook above as a CSV, reconciled to an identity it states about itself: `Win / Loss` is WIN exactly when the yes votes exceed the no votes, in all 4,743 rows. scripts/extract_dls_overrides.py refuses to write if that ever stops holding.

items.title: Every file in the Finance Committee’s delivery, and what became of it
items.what: Written by us. One row per file in the October 2026 delivery, under the name the committee gave it: filed, redacted, withheld, already held, or a duplicate of another file in the same delivery, with its sha256 and where it now lives.

items.title: What was redacted or withheld, and why
items.what: Written by us. One row per document that arrived by request rather than off a website and that the screen flagged or could not read: the decision (publish, redact, withhold), the rule, how much was removed, the reason and who decided. The raw copy of anything redacted or withheld is held privately; this register never holds a redacted value, only where one was.

items.title: Which workbook each cherry sheet figure came from
items.what: One row per export rather than per figure. A year, a population and a direction identify a workbook, so repeating its name and sha256 on all 235,254 data rows cost 30 MB of a 46 MB file to say 72 things. `fetch_dls_cherry_sheet.py --check` refuses if any row’s group is missing from here.

items.title: Where these came from, and what they cannot do
items.what: Written by us. Records the exclusion of a tenth file supplied as Abington which contains Lunenburg’s data in all 102 cells, and states plainly that no denominator appears anywhere in these workbooks.

items.title: Objects in the bucket that the index no longer names
items.what: The bucket forbids deletion for ten years and cannot be listed, so a document that leaves the manifest — usually a rename — leaves an object behind that nothing can find or remove. This register names each one, matched by sha256 rather than by name, and says `superseded_by` where the same bytes are held under another key. That is the only remedy there is.

items.title: Documents in flight: fetched, not yet in the bucket
items.what: The register `scripts/ingest.py` writes when it stages a document and clears when the bucket has read it back and matched its sha256. It is TRACKED on purpose: while a row is in it, `check_archive_backed_up.py` refuses every destructive operation, so a failed push means the next run retries rather than the next run destroying.

items.title: Override and Underride Votes, every municipality
items.what: Every Proposition 2½ question the state records — 4,743 of them across 305 municipalities — with the date, the tallies, the department and the result. NO export address is recorded: the report is not linked from the Gateway front page and we did not make the request, so the publisher’s own filename is what a resident asks DLS for.

items.title: Which reading task each delivered file belongs to
items.what: Written by us, generated: every file in the delivery assigned to exactly one task, by scripts/build_fincom_tasks.py, which refuses if any file has none.

items.title: The Finance Committee’s files, as reading tasks
items.what: Written by us. One row per task for turning the delivery into tables: the documents it covers, what it produces, the check that makes it done, and its state. Progress is rendered in notes/generated/FINANCE-COMMITTEE-INGEST.md.

groups.title: The athletics ledger, obtained by records request
groups.blurb: Answered by the Town on 17 June 2026, to a request by a resident. These are the first documents in this archive that record money moving on a date — the cashbook of the athletics revolving fund for three full fiscal years — rather than a prior year re-presented inside next year’s budget argument. The request form is not published: it carries the requester’s home address and telephone number, and no figure depends on them. Provenance, the town’s own filenames and a sha256 for each file are in PROVENANCE.md, listed below.

items.title: FY26 year-to-date budget report, period 12 — as printed
items.what: The same report as MUNIS prints it, and the only one of the pair that states its own parameters: Year/Period 2026/12, Print totals only: N, Suppress zero bal accts: Y, Account type Expense, program glytdbud. The spreadsheet states no period at all, so the two are asserted to be one report by reconciling the spreadsheet’s 635 account rows to this file’s own printed GRAND TOTAL — expended $52,163,984.85 and encumbrances $529,325.69 agree to the cent. The three appropriation columns differ by under a dollar because this file rounds them and the spreadsheet does not, which settles something the project had only been able to back-solve: the rounding is in the printing, not in the ledger. The sender’s filename is “Print_ YEAR-TO-DATE BUDGET REPORT.pdf”.

items.title: Every Parks & Recreation programme offered in FY2025, as the public saw it
items.what: 32 pages from MyRec: each programme’s description, sessions, ages and fee. The catalogue the sales reports count against. Records request, August 2025.

items.title: Athletics by sport, three school years
items.what: The district’s own operating workbook: one row per sport, with participation counts by fee category and cost lines for officials, coaches, transportation, uniforms and the rest, for 23/24, 24/25 and 25/26. The only document here that puts a cost against a sport. It also states the high school fee for each year, which is how we learned the 2025-26 rate was $325 and not the $250 the model assumed. Its own totals do not all tie, and which ones do not is published alongside it. The town’s filename is Copy of Athletics 24.25 (1).xlsx.

items.title: FY26 year-to-date budget report, period 12 — spreadsheet
items.what: The first ACCOUNT-LEVEL general fund expenditure report in this archive. Every prior one was run with Print totals only: Y, which renders the whole school district as a single row; here it is 258 accounts, each with an org code, an object code and a description. Sent by Jennifer Warren, Town Manager, on 2 September 2026, produced the evening before by Karen Barrett, Town Accountant. The sender’s filename is “FY26 BUDGET YEAR TO DATE REPORT (9-1-2026).xlsx”. It carries the appropriation columns UN-ROUNDED, which the printed form does not. **Period 12, not 13** — June, with the books not yet closed; the Town Manager’s covering note says the figures “are likely to continue to adjust as we continue the year-end reconciliation process”. Zero balance accounts are suppressed, so an account absent here is not necessarily absent from the ledger.

items.title: A contractor’s bid for grounds maintenance at the parks, from 1 July 2024
items.what: One page: mowing, weeding, turf, clean-ups and infield work priced per park — Fitzgerald, McNally, Marshall, Memorial, Town Beach, Wallis — for year one. A bid, not an invoice; what was paid is in the FY2024 Parks budget report. Records request, August 2025.

items.title: Athletics revolving fund, journal detail, FY2024
items.what: The same export for FY2024, the year the fund’s cash fell by $103,852.53. Its opening balance is a row the town prints, which is what lets the three years be chained and checked. The town’s filename is FY24 Account_Detail_.xlsx.

items.title: Athletics revolving fund, journal detail, FY2025

groups.title: Our analyses
groups.blurb: What we concluded, written up so it can be argued with. These are the only documents here we wrote — everything else in this archive was published by somebody else. Where one of them turned out to be wrong, the correction is in the document rather than quietly removed.

items.title: The FY26 closeout analysis, rendered for reading on paper
items.what: A rendering of analyses/fy26-closeout.md, built by scripts/build_analysis_pdf.py. The markdown is the source; every figure in it is recomputed by scripts/verify_fy26_closeout.py.

items.title: What the town owed on 30 June, by purpose, FY2007–FY2025
items.what: The FIVE YEARS OUTSTANDING DEBT table out of fifteen annual reports — principal outstanding by purpose, split inside and outside the Chapter 44 debt limit. Each report prints five as-of years, so the series carries UP TO FIVE INDEPENDENT READINGS OF EVERY YEAR, taken up to four years apart, and they agree to the dollar in 18 of 19 years. The exception is FY2017, whose own report prints $51,797,859 six times and whose four successors all print $51,797,860; nothing here settles which is right, so both are kept. Publication is per column AND per section, because a scan that starts part-way down the table can carry every printed total while three purposes are physically off the image.

items.title: The same analysis, rendered for reading on paper
items.what: A rendering of analyses/connecting-the-budget.md, not a separate document and not a separate source. Built by scripts/build_analysis_pdf.py; a copy accompanies the request sent to the Town. If the two ever differ, the markdown is the one every figure was verified against.

items.title: Show your work: every calculation, opened up
items.what: The method document. Every figure this project publishes, with its inputs, the formula, a worked example in real dollars, and — beside each one — whether it is somebody else’s figure, a contract, a statute, our measurement or our assumption. Fifteen sections: the projection itself, why each escalator is what it is, special education, out-of-district tuition, health insurance, free cash, athletic fees, the levers, the cut cascade, the tax base and overrides, an assumption register ranked by what each one moves, and what none of it can compute. GENERATED from the live model by scripts/build_show_your_work.py, so it cannot drift from the code — run it with --check to prove the copy you are reading is current. Written to be usable by an assistant checking a number as well as by a resident following the argument.

items.title: How Lunenburg compares: neighbours, peers, look-alikes and destinations
items.what: Four comparison sets, because they answer four questions: the six towns that share a border (computed from Census boundary polygons, not remembered), the five this project uses as peers, the towns the math picks out of all 351, and the places Lunenburg children are actually schooled. The finding the two cohorts exist for: no town is among the ten closest to Lunenburg on both what it IS and what it DOES.

items.title: What the town is worth, by class, and the levy on it
items.what: The Assessors’ tables out of FY2011-FY2025: valuation and levy by major class, new growth, average values, the LA4 totals and the levy build-up. 170 rows, 144 checked against three statements the tables make about themselves — the printed TOTALS row, the percent column summing to 100.0000, and `valuation x rate / 1000 = levy` on every class row. IT IS A SECOND READING OF A FAMILY ALREADY EXTRACTED, deliberately: `report-valuation.csv` covers the same pages and every one of its 321 rows is `no check`, because the Assessors print three or four tables on one page and one column ruler cannot serve them — FY2018 came out with a Commercial valuation of `6603477819.70`, which is the valuation and the tax rate run together. THE FY2021 PAGE REPRINTS FY2020’S TOTALS ROW: its four class rows are consistent to the penny and sum $194,412,308 above the total printed beneath them, which is FY2020’s figure exactly. Written `check failed` rather than corrected.

items.title: The stabilization funds, and who may spend them
items.what: What the town holds in reserve, which of it could lawfully go to an operating deficit — the general Stabilization Fund may, by a two-thirds Town Meeting vote, and the special purpose funds may not — and the four questions about movement the archive cannot yet answer because the balances are extracted but unreconciled. Generated by scripts/build_stabilization.py.

items.title: The cable fund: what Comcast pays, and what it buys
items.what: FY2015-FY2025, and NOTHING IN THIS ARCHIVE HELD ANY OF IT until now — it was found because two of its pages had been classified as enrollment and one as payroll. It is rule 11 in miniature: cable licence money paying real salaries, in no budget line anybody votes on, so a reader of the town’s appropriations cannot see the people it employs. 147 of 165 rows tie to a printed total. Three years disagree with themselves and are recorded rather than reconciled: FY2017’s printed TOTAL omits a $450.00 vendor expense, FY2025’s ending balance is beginning less expenses and ignores the year’s own $262,565 of revenue, and FY2020 and FY2024 each print their expenses twice on one page with the two copies disagreeing.

items.title: What the town was still owed on 30 June, levy by levy
items.what: The Collector’s RECEIVABLES SUMMARY out of the annual reports: one row per tax levy and charge, eight columns from BALANCE FORWARD through COMMITTMENTS, ABATEMENTS, PAYMENTS, REFUNDS, TRANSFER and ADJUSTMENTS to BALANCES, ending in the town’s own printed GRAND TOTAL. 522 rows, and every one closes the table’s per-row identity. THE COLUMN ORDER CHANGES MID-ARCHIVE — FY2016-FY2018 print ADJUSTMENTS REFUNDS PAYMENTS ABATEMENTS and FY2019 onward print ABATEMENTS PAYMENTS REFUNDS TRANSFER ADJUSTMENTS — so four columns transpose silently for anyone who assumes one layout. And FY2023 and FY2024 are both headed `FY2021 COLLECTION OF TAXES`, a stale template; the fiscal year cannot be read off the heading.

items.title: Special education and the curve
items.what: The FY27 level-service budget rises 3.98%. Strip out one line — out-of-district tuition, budgeted down 46% — and it rises 6.23%. What that one-off is doing to the rate, and what it risks for FY28. Budget columns only; no actual spending is used anywhere in it.

items.title: The town departments and the schools, budget by budget, FY2010–FY2025
items.what: Written by us, from every general fund account in the Finance Committee’s files: how fast each side’s starting budget grew against the levy limit, with health insurance put on the same footing, who pulls on the gap, and who leaves money unspent. A DRAFT, unlisted, for review. Generated by scripts/build_department_budgets.py and recomputed by scripts/verify_department_budgets.py.

items.title: What Lunenburg spends for each pupil, and what that number hides
items.what: DESE’s all-funds per-pupil figures: Lunenburg against every district in Massachusetts and against five neighbours, FY2009–FY2025. The gap decomposed into a numerator and a denominator, into eleven function categories, and into pay against staffing — and the two Chapter 70 standings that look like a contradiction and are not one.

items.title: The athletics ledger: what a cashbook shows that a budget line cannot
items.what: Written from the records request answered on 17 June 2026 — the first dated record of money moving that this project has held for anything touching the school budget. The fund’s cash for three years, tied end to end against the opening balances the town itself prints. Four journal entries, described only as an adjustment made per a memo we do not hold, carry 65% of one year’s receipts. What the district’s own workbook says athletics cost, against what the town appropriated for it: 44% in FY2024. And why none of that measures special education, while still changing what we should believe about it. Every figure recomputed by scripts/verify_records_request_2026_06.py.

items.title: The Monty Tech assessment — the school bill nobody in Lunenburg votes on
items.what: Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical is the larger of the two routes out of Lunenburg’s own schools and the only school line the town does not vote. What sets the assessment: the Chapter 70 minimum required local contribution, derived from DESE’s own workbook for FY2007–FY2026 and checked against DESE’s printed apportionment sheet and five figures stated at three public meetings. The four parts of the bill where the district publishes them, the twenty-year series with its eleven check-failed candidates drawn as candidates, and the town’s own forecast of the line against what it did. Every figure recomputed by scripts/verify_monty_tech.py.

items.title: Free cash: is Lunenburg hoarding, or rebuilding?
items.what: Two claims about the same number — that the town is too conservative, and that its free cash is not up to standard — set against the DLS proof for nine towns. It does not settle the argument, and says why in the first paragraph: a standard for free cash is a ratio and these files are a numerator. What it does establish is the shape. Two thirds of Lunenburg’s 2025 free cash is money appropriated and not spent, up from 31% in 2023 — a balance built from underspending is a different thing from one built from revenue beating forecast, and they imply different remedies.

items.title: Who runs the town: every elected seat, appointed seat and officer
items.what: The ELECTED OFFICIALS and APPOINTED OFFICIALS listing read as data, FY2022 to FY2025. Two thirds of the posts the town lists are unpaid seats on boards. It is NOT a headcount of town employees — a DPW labourer or a town hall clerk holds no appointed post — and it says so, because the wage list that would give a headcount stopped naming departments after FY2016.

items.title: Open seats: the town boards a resident could join
items.what: A LIST rather than a report — the one page here somebody reads and then does something about. Seats the town printed empty, then every filled seat by the year its term runs out. Regenerated by the daily refresh, and published as `/data/open-seats.json` so an assistant can answer the question directly.

items.title: Hiring here instead of placing there
items.what: Whether in-district special education staffing reduces out-of-district placements — the argument the district put on the record in August 2026, and why this project cannot model it. Placements fell from 30 in FY2015 to 10 in FY2025 while in-district spending rose; that is a correlation and four other explanations fit it equally well. A SCOPING NOTE, not a finished analysis: it has no verifier and nothing in it should be quoted as a finding.

items.title: Solution options: what the stabilization funds could do about the gap
items.what: The companion to the stabilization report, and deliberately separate from it: that page describes what the town holds, this one is only about what can be done with it. Three questions in order — can the town stop putting money in, can it spend what is already there, and then what. Spending the whole spendable balance closes two years and runs out partway through the third; stopping the deposits is recurring money, which is the right shape, and covers about a quarter of the first year’s gap. Neither closes it. The gap comes from model/finance.py, the balances from the town’s general ledger, the deposits from the articles that made them. See scripts/build_stabilization_option.py.

items.title: The FY27 budget and the override
items.what: Where things stand: the adopted budget, the four scenarios, what the balanced budget cut, the override result, the town’s revenue mechanics, and the first-cut FY28 arithmetic. The foundation the rest of this rests on.

items.title: How Lunenburg compares, and what matching would cost
items.what: Lunenburg spends less for each pupil than almost every district in the state — 310th of 318 in FY2025 — and this turns that rank into dollars: what reaching the median, or matching any named district, would cost. Also what the town itself is REQUIRED to raise for each pupil beside what the state sends, which is the figure the regionalisation argument actually turns on. Generated by scripts/build_spending_target.py.

items.title: The sixteen annual town reports, and what has been read out of them
items.what: Every financial page in every annual town report, what state it is in and what proved it. `proven` means the figures tie to something the page states about itself; `unproven` means the rows exist and nothing has checked them, which is NOT the same as wrong; `refused` means an extractor reached the page and wrote nothing; `blocked` means the page cannot be read at all. Generated by scripts/build_annual_reports.py from sources/data/annual-report-pages.csv, so its counts cannot drift from the queue they describe.

items.title: Budgets across town: every department, and which ones move the total
items.what: What Town Meeting voted for each of the twelve departments in the omnibus budget, for the three years the detail reconciles, beside the voted total for every year from FY2012. It refuses the question it is most often asked — an omnibus budget cannot show a deficit, because a town may not vote one — and answers the useful version instead: ten of twelve departments grew faster than the levy cap, and the schools are the biggest line without being the fastest.

items.title: Board composition: how the boards are made up, and how they turn over
items.what: Which bodies are biggest, how fast each changes hands, and whether the establishment is growing. The finding the charts exist for: the seats are nearly flat across ten years while about a third of the PEOPLE in them change every year, and the town-wide figure hides a spread from 65% to nothing.

items.what: One of the twelve departments in the omnibus budget, with every budget line the town prints beneath it for FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025, the lines reconciled against the department total the page prints, and the lines that moved most between the first year and the last. items.title: Who held which role, in every department, board and school
items.what: One row per person per role per year, assembled from four readings of the annual reports: the officials listing for boards and appointed posts, the Police and Fire rosters, the four schools’ rosters, and the departments that name their staff in prose. `status` keeps PEOPLE and POSTS apart — `filled` is a named person, `vacant` is a seat the town prints as empty, and `post` is an establishment position a department states without ever saying who fills it, which is how the DPW and the Assessing office publish. Building it was a test of the data model rather than a presentation of it, and it found seven classes of defect nothing that COUNTS things had: a listing footnote read as a post, sub-headings promoted to bodies, and one post under four spellings. Rendered at /org-charts.

items.title: The town’s wage list, name by name — AN INCOMPLETE READ
items.what: Every name and amount the annual report’s `Town & School Employee Gross Wages` list prints, for the years it reads. NOTHING ON THE SITE USES IT AND nothing should until it reads in full: four years come back near-complete (FY2017, FY2020, FY2021, FY2025) and six read badly or not at all, and the list is set in two columns whose second column loses its given names, so a third to a half of the entries cannot be matched to a person. A department total built on it would rank the scan rather than the payroll. TJ: *“if we dont have the data, we shouldn’t show partial data. that may be misleading”* — so it is held here as working material, and the two things it would answer are registered in money-gaps.csv instead.

items.title: Who works for the DISTRICT today, off the six sheets the schools publish
items.what: 527 rows across six listings: the district’s roll-up of every employee and the five the District Office and the four schools keep themselves. THE GRAIN IS A PERSON AS ONE LISTING PRINTS THEM, never a person — somebody two buildings both list has two rows, which is the whole reason the per-school addresses were gathered, and folding them together would delete the finding. The first people-source here covering the district from OUTSIDE an annual report, and the first carrying an identifier rather than a name: 450 rows have an address the sheet prints, 55 one derived from the rule Turkey Hill’s own sheet states, and 22 nothing but a name. IT IS A CONTACT LIST — no FTE, no funding source, no reporting line, and no date beyond the day it was fetched, which is the only date any of the six has.

items.title: Every town post and who held it, FY2022 to FY2025
items.what: Read out of the ELECTED OFFICIALS and APPOINTED OFFICIALS listing in each annual report: every board and appointed post, its holders and their term-expiry years. Split the town’s own way — elected board seat, appointed board seat, appointed officer — from the section header and from whether the post states a membership. `size_check` splits the rows three ways against the size each heading states, and nothing may be counted without splitting on it.

items.title: Every Town Meeting article and how it was voted
items.what: FY2011 onward: the article, its subject, the result, the amount as printed, what the Finance Committee and Select Board recommended, and the verbatim quote with the page it was read from.

items.title: How long each named person stayed, by body and year
items.what: One row per person per body: the first and last year their name appears, how many years the BODY published in between, the years inside that span it published nothing, and whether they are CENSORED at either edge of the archive. Half of them are: somebody in a body’s first published year began before FY2011 and nothing here can say when, and somebody in its last is still there as far as this can see — so their tenure is a LOWER BOUND, not a length. Identity is surname plus first initial within one body, which merges `Josh`/`Joshua Tocci` and `Steve`/`Stephen McKenna`; the 79 pairs that choice joins are printed on every run and are nicknames rather than collisions.

items.title: The town’s wage grid — grade by step, as the annual reports print it
items.what: 939 rates. EVERY ONE CARRIES WHAT CONFIRMS IT in `confirmed_by`, because the pages are scans and a schedule prints no total to foot against: the check is a SECOND printing of the same grid, usually the following year’s town meeting booklet at that year’s stated cost-of-living article. A rate no second document confirms is in the refusals file instead of here.

items.title: Every debt issue’s repayment schedule, year by year to maturity
items.what: 831 rows off the annual reports’ debt pages. `column_foots` states, per row, whether the printed columns add up — and says `interest out by -1` where they miss by a dollar rather than smoothing it, because a rounding difference the town printed is the town’s. `due_fy` is the year a payment falls due and runs past this archive to FY2047; `report_fy` is the book it was printed in. Joining on the wrong one of those credits pages in reports that do not exist yet.

items.title: The Police and Fire rosters, by name, as the town prints them
items.what: Both departments list every officer and firefighter by rank and assignment in every annual report. Read from the WORD geometry because both are set in two columns. The Fire Department also states its strength in a sentence, so the book gives the same quantity twice and `roster_check` records whether the two agree — in most years they do not, and the difference is published rather than averaged away.

items.title: Every department the town lists, and where its report is
items.what: The CONTENTS PAGE of each annual report, read as data: one row per department per year, with the pages its report occupies — or the town’s own words, `No Report Submitted`, where there is none. This is the town’s department list rather than ours, which is why Facilities is on it; every list in this project before it was typed from memory. The page numbers are PRINTED page numbers and the offset to the PDF differs per year, so it is measured from the numbers each book prints at its own feet.

items.title: What each department says about its own staff, on its own pages
items.what: For every department-year in `report-index.csv`, its own pages read for a headcount in any of the six forms the town uses. Where there is no number the row carries a REASON — `mentions staff, states no number` or `no mention of staff on its own pages` — because those are different problems and a blank cannot tell them apart.

items.title: Cells read off the page image, and cells checked against it
items.what: Two kinds of row. `read` says OCR got a cell wrong and gives what the page prints, with the page that was looked at. `attested` says OCR got it RIGHT and the DOCUMENT is what does not add up — FY2023 prints a General Government total 80 cents under its own lines — so nobody re-reads a page hunting a fault that was never there. A row matching nothing fails the extractor.

items.title: What the Capital Planning Committee asked for, ranked, FY2015-FY2023
items.what: The Committee’s own ranked recommendation, which EXTENDS `capital-plan-fy27.csv` back nine years. A different table from `report-capital-projects.csv`, which is the fund balance schedule. Every year’s layout differs, so no column is named by position and none by heading: THE COST COLUMN IS THE ONE THAT FOOTS TO THE TOTAL THE PAGE PRINTS. 201 of 203 rows checked. FY2016 prints two totals — the Committee’s $780,975 for twelve projects and the Town Manager’s $619,475 for the first ten — and this holds the Committee list, so what was ASKED and what was FUNDED stay separate quantities.

items.title: FY26, as the books stood in June
items.what: The first account-level ledger this project has held, read line by line. The school department was $482,101 under budget at period 12 — the small remainder of $1,683,534 unspent across 160 accounts against $1,201,433 overspent across 56. Carries the kindergarten paraprofessional question: the FY26 approved budget published a −100% cut to that line, $99,064 was spent on it anyway with no appropriation and no transfer, and three readings fit the record equally well. Period 12 is NOT the year-end close, so nothing in it is a surplus. Every figure is recomputed by scripts/verify_fy26_closeout.py; a PDF is published beside it.

items.title: Special education costs, and the size of a mid-year surprise
items.what: Our analysis. In-district and out-of-district special education, FY2010-FY2026: what was voted against what was spent at the close, how large the overruns have been and so how large a mid-year reserve would have had to be, averages for each and combined, out-of-district cost per placed child as our labelled estimate, the circuit breaker beside it, and what the counts can and cannot say about mid-year movement. Generated by scripts/build_sped_costs.py and re-verified by scripts/verify_sped_costs.py. Unlisted while it is reviewed.

items.title: What each town department says about its own staffing, verbatim
items.what: Departments describe their staffing in the PROSE of their annual-report sections — no heading names it in any year, which is why it went unread. The sentence is stored as printed because that is the source; counts are parsed into their own columns only where the form is unambiguous, and a statement that cannot be counted still gets a row with `parsed=no`. The forms do not agree with each other — a count and a range from the Fire Department, an establishment post by post from the DPW, a list of names from the Building Department — so `measure` says which kind each row is and nothing may be summed across kinds.

items.title: The same Collector’s table, for the years read off a TEXT LAYER
items.what: The other half of `receivables.csv` and deliberately not a rival to it: it skips at runtime every year that file publishes, so the two partition the archive and together nine of fifteen years tie to the town’s own printed GRAND TOTAL in all eight columns. WHAT MADE THESE YEARS READABLE IS A SECOND INSTRUMENT, not a better parser — FY2014, FY2015 and FY2025 carry a real text layer, exact to the cent, and FY2014 is drawn sideways with no `/Rotate` so the rotation had to be measured. FY2025’s OCR returns 10 figures off a page holding 194. Every year read off a text layer ties; no year read off OCR does.

items.title: Athletics: what it costs and who pays
items.what: The one program where both sides of the money are visible, and therefore a test case for the whole budget: how far is an appropriation from what a thing costs? Very far. The district published athletics against the revolving fund once, for FY19, and in every year that document reports as actual the fund paid more of athletic transportation than the town did. Also what an "actual" on this line really is — in the one ledger view we have, a purchase order with nothing yet paid. Verify with scripts/verify_athletics.py.

items.title: Who works for the town TODAY, off its own staff directory
items.what: 147 people across 27 departments, each with the title the town prints beside their name, from 28 pages at `/m/directory/department?did=N`. THE ONLY PEOPLE SOURCE HERE NOT READ OUT OF AN ANNUAL REPORT, which is why it was fetched: a department that files no report is invisible to both of the others and they share the blind spot. Four departments appear here and in neither — Accounting, Human Resources, Facilities/Grounds/Recreation and Public Access Cable. IT IS A CONTACT LIST, NOT AN ORG CHART: no rank order, no reporting line and NO DATE, so it is a snapshot rather than a series and a later fetch will silently differ.

items.title: Where a department publishes and we still have no number
items.what: The audit of the two readers above, one row per department per year. Every cell that is not a number is a to-do or an explanation, never a finding about the town. Rendered as a grid in notes/generated/STAFFING-COVERAGE.md.

items.title: The FY26 school surplus, from the period-13 ledger
items.what: Our analysis. What the school department left unspent in FY2026, read off the MUNIS period-13 report run on 6 October 2026: where it landed against the range the period-12 ledger allowed, account by account, what is still encumbered, where the unspent money sat by function, and what the School Committee was told in July. Generated by scripts/build_school_surplus.py --fy 2026 and re-verified. Unlisted while it is reviewed.

items.title: Budget versus actual
items.what: Did what the town budgeted match what it spent? Written for two readers — plain terms and the evidence, side by side. Deliberately separate from the app’s projection, and it says why. Unfinished: it names what it cannot see without the town’s accounting records.

items.title: Special education and the funds outside the budget
items.what: Special education as a cost driver, out-of-district tuition, the circuit breaker account, and the school and town money held outside the operating appropriation. Carries a correction notice at the top — two growth figures in it were derived on a basis we no longer stand behind.

items.title: FY26 on the town side, as the books stood in June
items.what: The same account-level ledger read for the other 67 departments. Snow removal cost $1,038,092 against an appropriation of $355,571 — 292% — while the town’s $185,000 Reserve Fund went entirely unused. $3.3M left the operating budget for capital and stabilization. And $1,262,376 of school retiree health insurance sits in a town department, invisible in the school budget, which is part of why DESE’s all-funds figure exceeds the appropriation. The town overspends on 18 of 376 accounts where the schools overspend on 57 of 259 — a fact with four explanations and no way here to choose between them. Period 12, so nothing in it is a surplus. Verified by scripts/verify_fy26_closeout_town.py.

items.title: Is anyone sitting on money? Town and schools
items.what: Our analysis. Every pot of money the town and the schools hold outside the voted budget, as a balance at each 30 June for as many years as a document prints it: the schools’ fourteen fee, choice, lunch, gift and circuit-breaker funds FY2011-FY2026 (the later years carried through the MUNIS period-13 ledgers and proved against the March 2026 report), the school budget’s turnback at the close, free cash and its components, the town’s special revenue funds, and the general stabilization fund. Generated by scripts/build_sitting_on_money.py and re-verified by a second route. Unlisted while it is reviewed.

items.title: Are we spending what comes in? The school funds, FY2023 to FY2026
items.what: Our analysis. For every school fund outside the voted budget, revenue against expenditure for each closed year FY2023-FY2026 from the MUNIS period-13 ledgers, by kind (fees, school choice, lunch, gifts, circuit breaker, grants); which revolving funds cover their own booked spending; athletics set beside the general fund’s spending on the same function; reconciled to /analysis/sitting-on-money and to the FY2023 annual report. Generated by scripts/build_spending_what_comes_in.py and re-verified by a second route. Unlisted while it is reviewed.

items.title: The FY25 school surplus, from the closed ledger
items.what: Our analysis. What the school department left unspent in FY2025, read off the MUNIS period-13 report rather than the minutes: the turnback at the close, what moved out of the budget during the year, where the unspent money sat by function, and how it compares with the figure the School Committee was told. Every figure is generated and re-verified. Unlisted while it is reviewed.

items.title: How many names stop appearing, by body and year
items.what: One row per body per published year: the people in it, how many of them are absent from the NEXT year the body published, and the rate. MEASURED ACROSS PUBLISHED YEARS, never calendar years, because 27 of 86 bodies skip a year inside their own span and a naive count reads a missed report as the whole staff leaving and returning. A NAME LEAVING A ROSTER IS A NAME LEAVING A ROSTER: not a resignation, a retirement or a cut post, and not a separation rate.

items.title: Who chaired each board, from the body’s own report
items.what: The officials listing marks its chairs with asterisks under a footnote reading `** denotes chairperson`, and stops printing it after FY2016 — which left 274 bodies in the org chart with members and nobody at the top. The chairs did not stop being published; they moved into the reports: `Richard Letarte, Chairman`, `Chairperson Deb Lincoln`. 200 mentions across fourteen years and 46 bodies, attributed by the town’s own contents page. A CHAIR NAMED IN A REPORT IS A CHAIR THE REPORT NAMES: it is not a term of office and it is undated within the year, so a body that changed chair mid-year keeps two rows rather than being resolved. 53 bodies — the School Committee, the Library Trustees, the Board of Health — name no chair anywhere, which is registered as a gap rather than filled in.

items.title: Spent with no budget: school lines voted at $0, FY2023 to FY2026
items.what: Our analysis. Every school general fund line that spent money against a $0 budget in the MUNIS period-13 ledgers, FY2023-FY2026, by three separate definitions (voted at $0 and spent; still at $0 after transfers and spent; voted at $0 and funded by a mid-year transfer), which lines recur, and the FY2026 kindergarten aide lines as the worked case. Special funds excluded because they spend without appropriation by law. Generated by scripts/build_spent_no_budget.py and re-verified by scripts/verify_spent_no_budget.py. Unlisted while it is reviewed.

items.title: Who signed each department’s report — the head of every body, by year
items.what: The block that ends a department’s report: `Respectfully submitted, Sheila M. Harrity, Ed.D., Superintendent`. 184 of them across fourteen years, each a person, a title and a page. It is the ONLY place the town names the person in charge of a body that publishes no roster — the Library, the Town Clerk, Conservation, the Sewer Commission — and it exists because a claim that the district published no Superintendent after FY2012 was challenged and turned out to be about our extractor rather than about the town. INCOMPLETE: 104 rows carry the department, from the contents page; 80 do not, and those are attributable rather than absent (see A11 in notes/QUEUE.md). A TRAP: `Thomas R. Browne, Superintendent-Director` signs the Montachusett Regional report inside Lunenburg’s book and is a different district’s superintendent.

items.title: Where a document the town published is itself incomplete
items.what: TYPED BY HAND, because a defect in somebody else’s printing cannot be derived — it has to be found by a person and written down with its evidence. One row per defect: what is wrong, HOW IT WAS FOUND, and what in the document proves it. The first is the FY2022 annual report, whose Fire Department roster stops mid-entry at the foot of page 85 and omits the call firefighters entirely — twelve names against a strength the same report states as forty. Read alongside `roster-completeness.csv`, which measures the shortfall, and `money-gaps.csv`, which holds the questions nobody published an answer to. Keeping the three apart is the point: a defective document, a thin reading of ours, and an unpublished fact are three different things.

items.title: What each board adopted as its goals, and when
items.what: One row per objective: the board, the fiscal year, the goal and objective text, the thread it belongs to, and the meeting that adopted it with its date and address.

items.title: Where every fiscal year stands in the ingestion pipeline
items.what: One row per fiscal year and table family, and a step from 1 to 7: the PDF held, OCR run, text present, tables located, extracted to CSV, loaded to the database, used in a report. Every cell is derived from the artefact it describes, so it cannot go stale the way a hand-kept list does. It exists because the same question — which years do we have for this fund — was answered three different ways from three different artefacts in one afternoon, each true about the artefact and false about the archive.

items.title: Appropriation lines from the pages the main extract could not take whole
items.what: 32 lines. THE PROOF IS ON EVERY ROW and names which columns were tested and which were not — a subtotal often prints an encumbrance and a balance that the lines above it do not, so those two are untested by construction and the row says so instead of implying otherwise.

items.title: The matters this project tracks across boards
items.what: One row per thread: the question a resident is following, which boards touch it, the match rules that find it in the record, when it was registered, and whether it has closed and on what vote.

items.title: Where both debt tables came from, and every page that refused
items.what: Written by us, and generated, so its counts cannot drift. It lists the refusals rather than only the successes — including the one that matters most: FY2017 page 42 reads a currency sign as a `3` in two figures on one column, both gain exactly $30,000,000, and `principal + interest = TOTAL DEBT` then closes PERFECTLY at twenty times every other year on the page. An identity cannot see a compensating error, so the extractor refuses a figure more than eight times the median of its own row and calls that a guard rather than a proof.

items.title: Which bodies file an annual report, and which say they did not
items.what: One row per body: the years it filed, and the years the contents page printed `No Report Submitted` beside its name in the town’s own words. 612 filings and 40 of those refusals across fourteen books. THE THIRD STATE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: a body that is not on the contents page at all has refused nothing, and four real departments are on none in any year, so reading their silence as a refusal would be a statement about them rather than about the document.

items.title: What other districts did
items.what: The comparison across neighboring districts, and the order in which things actually get cut when an override fails.

items.title: The district’s job postings, as a history: what was listed, and when it left
items.what: Written by us, from the snapshots of Lunenburg Public Schools’ own SchoolSpring account (employer 11047) that `fetch_school_job_postings.py` takes daily, one row per posting keyed on SchoolSpring’s job id. Post, display and closing dates are the publisher’s. `first_seen`, `last_seen` and `removed_seen` ARE OURS: they are the days we looked, bounded by the fetch cadence, never the day a post went up or came down. A REMOVAL IS NOT A HIRE — a posting leaves when it is filled, closes, is withdrawn or is reposted, and nothing here says which. Pay is printed only where the district shows it.

items.title: How many of a body’s people the org chart holds, against the town’s own count
items.what: A shortfall is only a fact when something the town SAID supplies the denominator, so every row carries its basis and the sentence it was read from: a stated headcount (the Library, FY2019 — *“we only employ ten total”*), a stated career-and-on-call strength (the Fire Department, low end always), or an establishment of posts with no names (the DPW, the Assessing office). The gross-wages list would be the best denominator here and is EXCLUDED: its department column is read for 156 rows of 2,866, and against it the Fire Department shows five paid and forty-five named — a statement about our extractor, not about the town.

items.title: The Public Employees Committee agreement, event by event
items.what: Dated events in the town’s PEC agreement — the body that governs health insurance plan design and the contribution split under c.32B §§21-23 — each with the verbatim quote it rests on and the document it came from.

items.title: What connects the school budget to the Town’s books, and what does not
items.what: How far a dollar can be followed from what was budgeted to what was spent. It works for the department as a whole — both school departments reconcile to $1.93 — and by category, where 41 of the budget’s 45 function codes meet the code carried inside the Town’s account numbers. It stops below that: MUNIS shortens account names to ten characters, so MS GUIDANC and HS GUIDANC are both 2710 where the budget has a row per school, and no single line can be followed into the ledger by anyone, inside the Town or outside it. The category comparison holds for FY2026 period 12 and no other period, because that is the one report that arrived as a spreadsheet rather than a PDF — the printed form drops the account string, and the account string is the join.

items.title: Every year of that table, published or refused, with the reason
items.what: Written by us. Twelve readings: six tie to their printed GRAND TOTAL on all eight columns, and six are refused with the instrument failure named — a header returned as one box, a scan that stops before BALANCES, a dropped BALANCE FORWARD column. Each is our reading failing, not the town declining to print: all of them publish the table and all of them print a total. IT ALSO CARRIES THE ONLY CHECK HERE THAT TESTS A YEAR AGAINST SOMETHING OUTSIDE ITSELF — articulation, where one year’s closing balance must be the next year’s opening. Every consecutive pair ties to the cent except one: FY2018 opens $13,300.00 above where FY2017 closed, in two printed grand totals in two different books. Recorded, not explained.

items.title: The people more than one Lunenburg school lists as its own
items.what: Written by us, from the row above. 28 people in FY2027, one of them on four listings. TWO ENCODINGS, BOTH KEPT: the roll-up writes sharing into a free-text school column (`Primary School & THES`) and the buildings write it by repetition, and they agree about five of the 28. Most of the apparent disagreement is the roll-up’s combined value `Lunenburg Middle High School` for the building the two upper schools share — structure, not noise. WHAT IS MEASURED IS THE REPETITION; “a shared specialist” is a hypothesis and nothing here tests it, since no sheet says what fraction of a post sits in which building.

items.title: What falls due in each future year, out to FY2047
items.what: THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME QUANTITY, AND KEPT APART FROM IT. Outstanding debt is principal owed on a date; this is debt service falling due in a year — a different stage, and flattening the two would be rule 1’s error in a new coat. Only the GRAND TOTAL block publishes: twenty-odd narrow columns of small type come back from the scanner as `52782335 52547440 52531098`, so no individual bond issue can be footed. And the overlap between reports is MOVEMENT, not disagreement: FY2011 shows $155,945 due in FY2032 and FY2021 shows $2,303,500, because two school bonds were issued in between.

items.title: The thirteen years it will not publish, and why each refuses
items.what: Written by us, one line of reason each, and the reasons are not interchangeable. Six are refused because another extractor already proved them. FY2016 and FY2019 are CROPPED rather than faint — the BALANCES column is off the right edge of every page of FY2019 — which is a different remedy from the OCR losses, and asking the Town for an uncropped copy is the one that would work. Three more are torn by non-linear scan distortion at the foot of the page, exactly where the GRAND TOTAL row is, so the control that would prove them is the thing the scan destroyed.

items.title: Every change we saw to a district job posting, one row per event
items.what: Written by us, from the same snapshots as the row above: `posted` (first listed), `edited` (one row per field that differs between two looks, with the before and after -- descriptions compared as text, whitespace ignored), `relisted` and `removed`. `date` IS THE LOOK THAT SAW IT and `prev_look` the one before; the district made the change somewhere between the two, and the data cannot narrow it further. Pay is compared as SchoolSpring displays it, so a change to a figure the district hides is not an event here.

items.title: Thread candidates that were rejected, and why
items.what: The counterpart to threads.csv, kept because a rejected candidate is a decision rather than an absence: what was proposed, who declined it, the reason, and what would justify revisiting it.

items.title: Extractions that ran, refused to publish, and why
items.what: When a column will not foot to the total its own page prints, the reading is refused — and this is where the refusal is kept, with the amount it missed by. Without it a year read-and-refused looked exactly like a year nobody had opened, and five of them were being read and dropped on every run with the diagnosis printed to a terminal nobody was watching. A blocked year with a stated residual is a finite piece of work; a blank is a mystery.

items.title: Where Lunenburg sits, measure by measure
items.what: Twelve measures, each drawn as the full spread of the 161 towns that run their own K–12 district, with the middle half shaded. A rank is a fact; whether that position is remarkable needs the spread, and this is the spread.

items.title: Who Lunenburg is compared with, and where they are
items.what: Every Massachusetts town outlined from the Census TIGER polygons, with the towns this report names filled and pinned at their published centroids. Nothing on it is placed by eye.

items.title: Every Massachusetts town, shaded by one measure
items.what: The whole state as a choropleth, Lunenburg outlined in red. Shaded by RANK rather than by amount, because on nearly every measure here a handful of towns hold most of the total and the raw range would leave the other 350 an identical pale. The web version switches between thirteen measures; this is the one the report is about, spending per pupil, where Lunenburg is among the palest towns in the state.

items.title: What the town votes for, as a town
items.what: The budget report’s SIGNATURE image: each voted department drawn as a thing it buys — a schoolhouse, a police car, a dump truck — one icon for every million dollars. Repeated rather than scaled, because nobody can judge area. It makes the RANGE legible in a way a pie cannot: the largest department is 313 times the smallest, so four of the twelve are drawn as a fraction of a single icon.

items.title: Everyone the town publishes a count for
items.what: This report’s SIGNATURE image, and the one a reader remembers: every department that publishes a headcount drawn as rows of figures, one figure for every ten people. Repeated rather than scaled, because nobody can judge area — twenty-five school figures beside four fire figures is a ratio anyone can count. A department short of a whole unit is drawn as a PART figure rather than rounded, so the three-person Assessing office is neither inflated to ten nor erased.

items.title: Every body, its org chart and its money page — the join between the two
items.what: Written by us. 63 bodies; 34 reach a money page and 32 a board page, so /org-charts and /departments link both ways instead of a reader having to know the other exists. THE JOIN IS ON A NAME, which is the weakest kind there is, so every row states its `basis` and the generator FAILS if the match count falls — a join that silently matches less is indistinguishable from a body that stopped existing. Ten pairs are matched by hand and say so: the chart names the office (`Accounting Department`) and the finance registry names the officer who owns the account (`Town Accountant`), and no normalisation reaches from one to the other. A BODY WITH NO MONEY PAGE CARRIES THE REASON rather than a blank — most of the 23 are advisory committees the town votes nothing to, and which of them are that against a name spelled two ways is printed on every run and not guessed at.

items.title: The stabilization funds, each on its own scale
items.what: The same three funds as small multiples on a shared time axis. Each panel is stretched to its own range and prints that range, because against a $2.6M axis the Zoning Incentive fund is a flat line and its flatness is a finding rather than a rendering artefact.

items.title: Where each town’s school money comes from
items.what: Pupils, then dollars spent on each pupil split four ways: what the town must raise from homes, from business, what the state adds, and what it spends above the figure the state calculates for it. The four parts sum exactly to the spending they explain, and the last is the one a town meeting decides.

items.title: How many people each part of the town employs
items.what: The same data the ranked bars used to carry, drawn in figures: one row per department, one figure for every ten people, a PART figure where a department does not reach ten. TJ: the icon one is more interesting than the basic bar chart and is identical data wise.

items.title: The stabilization funds compared, on one scale
items.what: Ending cash for the three stabilization funds with a long enough proven series, at every year this archive has checked against the annual report’s own arithmetic. A dashed segment spans years not yet proven, so the line never asserts a path through a year nobody has read.

items.title: Every department that publishes a headcount, on one axis
items.what: The companion to the small multiples, and the one that answers SIZE rather than movement: every department on one people axis, so the schools dwarf the rest the way they do in the budget. Spaced by YEAR and broken at any year a department published no figure, because these series have holes in them and an unbroken line would draw a record the town never printed.

items.title: Headcount over time, where the town publishes one
items.what: One small panel per department with two or more published years, each on its own scale and spaced by YEAR so a year the department printed no figure — the Council on Aging in FY2012, FY2013 and FY2021 — shows as the gap it is. A hollow point is a year dropped as a misreading and is never drawn through.

items.title: Chart: the schools’ fourteen funds by kind, FY2011-FY2026
items.what: Our chart, generated with the sitting-on-money analysis: circuit breaker, school choice, lunch, fee-funded revolving funds and gifts, stacked by year end.

items.title: Every department, year by year
items.what: Twelve small panels, one per department, each on its OWN vertical scale so the shape of a $80,000 line is as legible as a $25M one. Eleven rise; only maturing debt falls.

items.title: Chart: each school fund, in minus out, by year
items.what: Our chart, generated with the spending-what-comes-in analysis: the fourteen fee, choice, lunch, gift and circuit-breaker funds, one cell per year.

items.title: Chart: money in and money out of the school funds, by kind, FY2023-FY2026
items.what: Our chart, generated with the spending-what-comes-in analysis: one panel per kind, revenue beside expenditure for each closed year.

items.title: Chart: what each pot held at each 30 June
items.what: Our chart, generated with the sitting-on-money analysis: one panel per pot, one dollar scale, so whether each is growing reads at a glance.

items.title: Chart: FY26 school budget against spending, by category
items.what: Our chart, generated with the FY26 school surplus analysis: each category’s revised budget split into spent, still committed and left over.

items.title: FY26 school department: the biggest misses, both directions
items.what: A diverging bar chart, the seven largest overspends and the seven largest underspends on one zero line. Deliberately not a pie: two of the three questions these charts answer are about VARIANCE, a signed quantity, and a pie cannot show a negative. Colours were run through a palette validator rather than chosen by eye. Rebuild with scripts/build_closeout_charts.py.

items.title: Chart: the special education overrun, year by year
items.what: Our chart, generated with the special education costs analysis: each year's overrun against the voted lines, the basis of the reserve figure.

items.title: FY26 town: the biggest misses, both directions
items.what: The same diverging bar for the town side, where 18 accounts overspend against the school department’s 56.

items.title: Chart: FY25 school budget against spending, by category
items.what: Our chart, generated with the FY25 school surplus analysis: each category’s revised budget split into spent, still committed and left over.

items.title: Chart: out-of-district tuition by who paid it, beside the circuit breaker
items.what: Our chart, generated with the special education costs analysis: tuition each year split into the general fund, the circuit breaker account and other funds, with the state's circuit breaker payments by year received and by the year whose costs earned them.

items.title: Payroll pages that would not read, and why each refused
items.what: Written by us. Two pages, both a PAIRING failure rather than a faint scan: FY2011 p98 pairs 80 half-rows and refuses 71, reading 93 names against 138 money figures; FY2012 p114 reads 131 money figures and not one personal name, so the department words left on it cannot be attributed to anybody. Neither was guessed at — an amount beside the wrong name is worse than an amount nobody has.

items.title: All twelve departments on one axis
items.what: The same figures as the small multiples, on ONE dollar scale, which is the point: the school line is most of the budget and ten departments share the floor. Growth is read on separate scales; size is read here.

items.title: Who gets the money: the voted budget split twelve ways
items.what: A pie of one fiscal year’s omnibus budget by department, ranked, every share also printed in the legend and in the table beneath. It answers the question a resident opens the page with — which department is biggest — which the pull chart deliberately does not.

items.title: Chart: each school line that spent against a $0 vote
items.what: Our chart, generated with the spent-with-no-budget analysis: one bar per line, largest first, split by the year it happened in.

items.title: Chart: where the FY26 school surplus was left, by category
items.what: Our chart, generated with the FY26 school surplus analysis: net unspent by plain-English category, largest first, coloured by our discretionary / circumstantial split.

items.title: Chart: where the FY25 school surplus was left, by category
items.what: Our chart, generated with the FY25 school surplus analysis: net unspent by plain-English category, largest first, coloured by our discretionary / circumstantial split.

items.title: Posts by kind, ten years — three nearly flat lines
items.what: Elected seats, appointed seats and officers over FY2016-FY2025. The shape IS the finding: the establishment barely changes while about a third of the people in it turn over every year.

items.title: Where the town’s seats are, by body
items.what: A pie of every filled post, ten largest named and the long tail grouped. It found a defect the table had hidden: a body called `MILES` with 27 members, which was the town PROFILE page read as a roster.

items.title: Where the town’s seats are, by body
items.what: A pie of every filled post in the listing, ten largest named and the long tail grouped. It found a defect the table had hidden: a body called `MILES` with 27 members, which was the town PROFILE page — `ROAD MILES- ABOUT 100` read as a heading and the prose beneath it read as people.

items.title: The gap each year, and what each stabilization option covers of it
items.what: One stacked bar per fiscal year, the whole bar that year’s level-service gap, split into the part the redirected deposits cover, the part the reserve covers, and the part still short. Both levers are pulled at once, which is the most favourable case there is; from FY31 the bar is almost entirely the part still short.

items.title: Money in and money out of the stabilization funds, by year
items.what: A diverging bar: deposits above the zero line, withdrawals below, one axis. It answers how OFTEN these funds are drawn on and for how much — eight withdrawals in thirteen years, none of them large beside the deposits. The balances are deliberately NOT on it: they are the same unit and thirty times the size, so showing them here would need a second y-axis.

items.title: FY26 town: where the money went
items.what: The ten largest town accounts by spending.

items.title: FY26 school department: where the money went
items.what: The ten largest accounts by spending, with everything else folded into one recessive bar.

items.title: Who the town employs, where it publishes a count
items.what: A pie at the head of the personnel report, the counterpart to the budget page’s. The whole is NOT the town: it is the people the town publishes a count for, and the subtitle says so, because a pie whose whole is unnamed is the shape that misleads.

items.title: Which town departments move the budget total
items.what: Diverging bars, one per department, in DOLLARS A YEAR above what the 2.5% levy cap would carry — the first version drew an index and called it points of total growth, which claimed an additivity it never had. It is the only chart on the page that puts employee benefits above the schools, which is the finding — a chart of SIZE would put the schools on top and say nothing.

items.title: How fast each department grows, against the levy cap
items.what: Compound annual change per department on one axis, with Proposition 2½ drawn on it. Ten of twelve bars extend past the cap. The cap limits the LEVY, not the budget — it is drawn because it is the line every board in this town argues against.

items.title: What Town Meeting voted, every year from FY2012
items.what: One column per fiscal year, from the GRAND TOTAL each annual report prints at the foot of its omnibus. The last column is amber because FY2026 is a total and nothing else: no department table is printed for it anywhere.

items.title: The stabilization reserve, drawn down against the school gap
items.what: The general Stabilization Fund from its opening general-ledger balance to empty, one column a year, with each year’s draw printed under the year. It does not taper — it stops, and the years after it stops are the point of the chart rather than padding on the end of it.

items.title: Chart: from the voted school budget to FY26 period 13
items.what: Our chart, generated with the FY26 school surplus analysis: voted, revised, spent and unspent at period 13, beside the period-12 floor and ceiling.

items.title: Combined balance sheets that would not publish, and what each failed
items.what: Written by us. Four pages, and the interesting ones are not faint scans. FY2023 p24 transcribes cleanly and passes three of four checks — every column foots to its own printed totals to the cent — and fails the fourth: its special revenue plus enterprise fund equity is $9,943,805.92 where the same report’s special revenue schedule prints $10,031,099.78 carried forward, a difference of $87,293.86 in a year four others agree to the cent. FY2024 p21 is the ENTERPRISE combining sheet, which is read and published elsewhere; the book’s own contents page sends a reader there for a town-wide sheet that is not in it. Every row names the document that would settle it.

items.title: Chart: town and school starting budgets, indexed to FY2010
items.what: The image the PDF and /docs copy carry; the web page draws it as a component.

items.title: Chart: in-district and out-of-district special education, by year
