items.title: How the ski co-op invoice reached us, and what it does not show
items.what: The provenance note for the invoice beside it: where it came from, its sha256, why it is `stated` rather than evidence, and the three things it does not establish — it is one season and says nothing about how earlier years split; it is a bill rather than a receipt, so it shows what the other towns were invoiced and not that they paid; and it does not say which account receives a reimbursement, which is what decides whether the money offsets the athletics line at all.

items.title: The FY27 capital programme, ranked by the town
items.what: All 22 projects the departments requested, in the Capital Planning Committee’s own rank order, with cost and the running total the town prints beside it — and a flag for the twelve that got funded. $3,267,208 requested against $1,830,203 funded, so $1,437,005 of ranked work is already below the line. That queue is why taking a dollar out of free cash costs a dollar of capital: nothing gains slack, the line just moves up. Rebuild with scripts/extract_capital_plan.py, which checks every row against the document’s own cumulative column and refuses to write if one disagrees.

items.title: Special education paraprofessionals, ten budgets
items.what: What the district budgeted for special education paras, FY18 to FY27, by school, read out of its own budget documents in the mirror above. Budget columns only, one budget stage held constant. The line grew 12.8% a year with an R-squared of 0.89 while the contract governing these staff gives 2.0% — which is the evidence the in-district escalator rests on. Rebuild with scripts/extract_budget_history.py.

items.title: Special education teachers, eight budgets
items.what: What the district budgeted for special education teachers, FY20 to FY27, by school. Grew 2.67% a year against a 3.5% agreement — below contract, which means fewer of them each year. The largest component of the in-district escalator, and the last one to stop being taken from a contract. Rebuild with scripts/extract_budget_history.py.

items.title: Out-of-district tuition, eleven budgets
items.what: What the district budgeted for out-of-district special education tuition, FY17 to FY27, read out of its own budget documents in the mirror above. Budget columns only, and one budget stage held constant throughout — a fiscal year has several budget figures for this line at different stages and they are far apart, so a series that took whichever number each document led with would be a walk across stages rather than a trend. Three of its years reproduce the FY27 workbook exactly. Rebuild with scripts/extract_tuition_history.py.

items.title: District total salaries, budget and actual by year
items.what: What the district budgeted for salaries and what it spent, FY14 to FY27, read out of its own budget documents in the mirror above. Both kinds of column are kept and labelled, which is what makes a budget-versus-actual comparison possible — and no projection reads the actual columns; scripts/audit_provenance.py fails the build if one does. Rebuild with scripts/extract_budget_history.py.

items.title: Figures the town stated about itself, with the quote
items.what: Not ours and not computed from anything here. The FY25 school surplus as the district stated it — $582,115.44 on 3 September 2025 and $603,885.97 on 17 September after purchase orders were closed — each with who said it, the minutes it is quoted from and the line number. Recorded separately from everything we derive, because the town’s closing figure is arrived at by closing its books and we cannot do that arithmetic from what we hold.

items.title: The ski co-op invoice, line by line and town by town
items.what: The invoice extracted: nine cost lines, the printed total and roster, and the four towns’ shares, each row carrying the workbook cell it came from. scripts/build_athletics_charts.py refuses to write unless the line items sum to the printed total, the towns’ shares sum to it, and their athletes sum to the printed roster — reconciling to the document’s own figures rather than to ours (rule 13).

items.title: District total expenses, budget and actual by year
items.what: The same for non-salary expenses. Read alongside the salary series in analyses/budget-vs-actual.md, which also records where the documents disagree with themselves.

items.title: Town Manager line-item budgets FY2024-FY2025, every version
items.what: Written by us: both FY24 preliminary versions, the FY25 line-item budget and five dated revenue-expense drafts, tied at every level, with anomalies logged by cell. Built by scripts/extract_town_budget_versions.py.

items.title: When each agenda and each set of minutes was MADE, from the document itself
items.what: 12,039 rows: the /CreationDate and /ModDate the town’s own PDFs and Word files carry, with the hours between a document being made and its meeting, and the days between a meeting and its minutes being made. A creation date is a LOWER BOUND on posting — a file cannot be published before it exists — and never the posting date, which the AgendaCenter does not publish. Written by scripts/extract_document_timestamps.py; read into the meeting record.

items.title: Every agenda and set of minutes the town has listed, and when we first saw it
items.what: Written by us, and it is an OBSERVATION LOG rather than a measurement — what this project’s crawler could see on the town’s AgendaCenter on a given day. One row per document, keyed on the town’s own file id. `first_seen` is the day OUR crawler first saw it and NOT the day the town posted it: the AgendaCenter publishes no posting timestamp, so any gap between a meeting and its minutes appearing is an upper bound bounded by how often we look. The 12,065 rows adopted when the watch was seeded carry an EMPTY first_seen, because we do not know — an empty cell rather than a guess — and the `basis` column says which rows those are. Rebuild with scripts/watch_meetings.py.

items.title: What every Massachusetts municipality spends on health insurance, FY2002 onward
items.what: 8,775 rows: one dollar figure per municipality per fiscal year, all 351, as filed on Schedule A Parts 2 and 6 and published by the Division of Local Services. TWO WARNINGS DLS PRINTS ITSELF: for a self-insured town the figure includes the employee share, and a town accounting through a trust may have workers’ compensation and OPEB inside it — and nothing in the file says which town is which, so the LEVEL is not comparable across towns and the growth is. Fetched by scripts/fetch_dls_property.py.

items.title: Which municipalities pay health claims from a trust rather than buying premiums
items.what: 8,424 rows, every municipality and fiscal year: the health trust fund’s starting balance, revenues, expenditures and fund balance as filed on Schedule A Part 6. It is the only published axis on which health spending can be told apart — a self-insured town’s expenditure figure includes the employee share. The report’s own Self-insured (Y/N) column is NOT reliable (Abington prints N every year while reporting millions through a trust), so the classification rests on whether the trust moved money. Fetched by scripts/fetch_dls_property.py.

items.title: The End of Year Financial Report, Schedule 3, by function and fund
items.what: Written by us. District totals by function across the general fund, grants and revolving funds, with the header cells each column name was built from. In the FY2024 working copy the grant columns evaluate to zero.

items.title: The school budget under the Town Manager’s FY2026 target, four versions
items.what: Written by us, from hand-built district workbooks: every line in every version, columns named from their headers, each version tied to its printed total. Built by scripts/extract_school_workbooks.py.

items.title: Tables read from Finance Committee presentations
items.what: Written by us: the tables extracted so far from slides and PDFs, each tied to the total it prints.

items.title: Special revenue, Chapter 90 and trust fund balances from the Finance Committee’s files
items.what: Written by us: the FY2020 special revenue funds, the Chapter 90 ledger, the FY2021 trust fund summary and the 2025 trust quarterlies, each tied to its own totals.

items.title: FY2027 department budgets as presented to the Finance Committee
items.what: Written by us: Police, Fire, Facilities, IT, Land Use and PACC worksheets, each tied to its printed totals.

items.title: Which words pin which page or document at the top of a search
items.what: Written by us. Topic tags for 77 pages and 259 documents so a search for a subject finds the page about it even where the word is not on it.

items.title: The town’s FY2020 fourth-quarter report, read off the scans
items.what: Written by us: only rows that prove both of the report’s own identities to the cent are published. Built by scripts/extract_fincom_records.py.

items.title: Whether the publisher’s copy is still our copy
items.what: The question underneath the one above. A link can still open and serve a different document — a Drive file can be replaced in place without its URL changing, and nothing in a link check would notice. So every address is fetched and the result compared to our copy by sha256. It also separates the ways bytes can differ without the document differing: a Google Doc is re-zipped on every export, and a PDF can be re-saved with a heading’s line-break in a new place. Only one of those is a change. Rebuild with scripts/verify_source_copies.py.

items.title: Whether each source document is still public
items.what: For every archived document that records where its publisher put it, whether that address still opens. On 29 August 2026 it mostly did not: 57 of 184 returned a Google sign-in wall, every one of them a Drive or Docs link, while the town’s own web server answered 81 of 81. The district was asked to reopen them and did — on 31 August the same 187 came back 186 open. Both readings are the archive’s reason for existing, measured. Rebuild with scripts/check_source_links.py.

items.title: The ski co-op invoice, 2025-26 season
items.what: The invoice Lunenburg High School’s athletic department issues to the other towns in the ski co-op, dated 30 March 2026. Lunenburg runs the co-op, pays the mountain and the coach, and bills Littleton, Narragansett and Leominster for their athletes: $12,392 gross, 14 skiers, of whom 3 are Lunenburg’s at $2,655.43 — 21.4% of the bill. It matters because the district’s by-sport workbook prints the whole co-op’s cost as the ski team’s cost, which makes ski the dearest sport per participation the town runs by comparing a four-town total with every other sport’s one-town total. A sheet the department assembled, not an accounting printout, so every figure off it is `stated` (rule 13a) — but it foots: the line items sum to its own printed total and the four towns’ shares sum to it too. Sent to this project by a resident; there is no publisher address, because the town does not publish it.

items.title: What Massachusetts law lets a town do about health insurance, and what it forbids
items.what: Eleven rows, one per option: the section of M.G.L. c.32B that permits or forbids it, who decides, the threshold, who the change lands on, and a link to the statute so a reader can check the sentence. Four of the eleven are things no town may do — cutting the employer share below 50%, changing the split through the 2011 plan-design process, revoking coverage, dropping retirees. The research behind it is notes/findings/MA-MUNICIPAL-HEALTH-INSURANCE.md.

items.title: What the schools say maintaining the fields and grounds costs, FY2024
items.what: Five rows from the Superintendent’s email of September 2026: about $126,000 of all fields and grounds work in FY2024 (including playgrounds, irrigation and the vehicles that also do snow removal), of which about $29–30,000 is vehicle and equipment maintenance, plus $9,500 autumn and $9,200 spring for the landscaper who mows the athletic grass fields and $19,400 for summer 2023 field repair. Every row is marked `stated`: these are figures a person read back from budget requests, not a printout from the books (rule 13a), and the fund’s own FY2024 expenditure is not in the archive to check them against. The Superintendent also states the outsourced mowing is paid from the Facility Revolving account — fund 1306, where the field rent is deposited.

groups.title: The town’s budget and finance documents, mirrored
groups.blurb: Every budget-relevant document linked from the town’s finance pages — 146 of them, including the audited financial statements and the year-end reports. Reached by walking the budget hub, town meetings and finances, and the finance-adjacent department pages rather than by enumerating the document store, which would have meant thousands of files about dog licenses.

Nothing was discarded: they are mirrored on the same terms as everything else, and several bear on the budget indirectly.

groups.title: The Open Meeting Law, as the State publishes it
groups.blurb: The statute (G.L. c.30A §§18-25), its regulations (940 CMR 29.00), the Attorney General’s guide, FAQ and checklists, and a chosen set of the AG’s determination letters — 773 documents, each the publisher’s own file. Held so that a quotation of the law can be checked against the law.

corpus.note: Every agenda and set of minutes the town publishes, across all boards. The extracted text is what the analysis reads and is what this site serves. The scanned originals — about 426MB — are archived too, and can be downloaded one at a time at /docs/minutes/<board>/<file>.pdf. They were never in the repository, so until September 2026 they existed on exactly one disk; they now have an off-site copy, which for an archive of public records that keeps losing its own links is the point.

note: Every document this analysis is built on. Nothing here is private or paid for. 45 came from the Town by records request and are marked; the rest were published by the district, the town, the state or a neighboring district. 5 of them are no longer open at the address their publisher used — checked 29 August 2026, and all but a handful were Google Drive links that now ask for a sign-in. Our copies stay open, and every row carries a sha256 so anyone who still has access can check them against the originals. Where a document was unreadable, or says something inconvenient, it is listed anyway.
